sources.label: ISO 13485 – Medical devices quality management systems
ISO 14971 – Application of risk management to medical devices

cards.title: Engineering meets medicine
cards.body:
A medical device has to work every single time, inside a human body or in the hands of a surgeon under pressure. That is why medical technology combines engineering and science with strict rules for design, testing and manufacturing.

In the lab you can try four interactive demos: how lenses correct vision, how the heart's electrical system works, how a knee implant moves, and how a device goes from idea to patient.

cards.title: Design controls & verification
cards.body: Development follows design controls: we capture user needs, turn them into design inputs (requirements), create the design, and then prove it works.
bullets: Verification – did we build the product right? (it meets every requirement)
Validation – did we build the right product? (it meets user needs in real use)
Human factors – the device must be easy and safe to use correctly

cards.title: Risk management & quality systems
cards.body:
Risk management (ISO 14971) runs through the whole life of a product: we identify hazards, estimate risks, reduce them and check that the remaining risk is acceptable.

Our quality management system follows ISO 13485. In the United States the FDA's Quality Management System Regulation (QMSR), in force since February 2026, aligns the FDA requirements with ISO 13485.

cards.title: Safe for the body
cards.body: Materials that touch the body are tested for biocompatibility (ISO 10993). Many products are sterilised – for example with ethylene oxide, radiation or steam – and the sterile barrier packaging must keep them sterile until use.

cards.title: Approval and life on the market
cards.body:
Before a product can be sold it needs approval or clearance – for example FDA 510(k), De Novo or PMA in the United States, or CE marking under the EU Medical Device Regulation (MDR).

After launch we keep watching: post-market surveillance collects complaints, adverse events and real-world data, so we can keep improving and act fast if needed.

demos.title: Optics – correcting vision
demos.text: Light must focus exactly on the retina for a sharp image. In a nearsighted (myopic) eye the focus lands in front of the retina. A diverging (minus) lens moves the focus back onto the retina. Choose an eye and adjust the correcting lens.
points: Contact lenses and spectacles correct refractive errors
In cataract surgery the clouded natural lens is replaced by an intraocular lens (IOL)
Lens power is measured in dioptres (D)

demos.title: Electrophysiology – the heart's wiring
demos.text: Each heartbeat starts with an electrical impulse from the sinus node that spreads in an orderly wave. In atrial fibrillation (AFib) the upper chambers fire chaotically. In catheter ablation, doctors use a 3D map to find the problem areas and create small lesions that block the faulty signals.
points: 3D mapping shows electrical activity and catheter position in real time
Ablation energy: radiofrequency, cryo or pulsed field
Pulmonary vein isolation is a common AFib treatment

demos.title: Biomechanics – knee replacement
demos.text: In a total knee replacement the worn joint surfaces are replaced. A metal femoral component glides on a polyethylene insert that sits on a metal tibial tray. Bend the knee to see how the parts move together.
points: Common materials: cobalt-chrome, titanium, highly cross-linked polyethylene
Implant design balances stability and natural movement
Robotic-assisted systems help plan and place implants

demos.title: Product lifecycle – idea to patient
demos.text: Every device follows a controlled lifecycle. Select a stage to learn what happens there.
points: Documentation is kept for every stage
Risk management runs through all stages
Quality is built in, not inspected in

lifecycle.title: Concept
lifecycle.text: Understand the unmet clinical need, the users and the use environment. Define user needs.

lifecycle.title: Design controls
lifecycle.text: Translate user needs into design inputs, create the design and review it at each phase.

lifecycle.title: Verification & validation
lifecycle.text: Test that the design meets its requirements (verification) and the users' needs (validation).

lifecycle.title: Clinical evidence
lifecycle.text: Collect clinical data that shows the device is safe and performs as intended.

lifecycle.title: Regulatory approval
lifecycle.text: Submit evidence to authorities – e.g. FDA or an EU notified body – to obtain clearance or approval.

lifecycle.title: Manufacturing
lifecycle.text: Transfer the design to production with validated processes and controlled suppliers.

lifecycle.title: Post-market
lifecycle.text: Monitor real-world performance, handle complaints, and improve the product.
